title: operator.iconcat() and operator.concat() accept a right operand that is not a sequence
body:
### Bug report

The docs describe both functions for two sequences: `a = iconcat(a, b)` "is equivalent to `a += b` for *a* and *b* sequences", and `concat(a, b)` returns "`a + b` for *a* and *b* sequences" ([`operator.rst`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.12.13/Doc/library/operator.rst?plain=1#L205-L208), [`#L500-L503`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.12.13/Doc/library/operator.rst?plain=1#L500-L503)). Neither implementation checks *b*, so `iconcat()` succeeds whenever the left operand's `+=` does:

    import operator
    print(operator.iconcat([1], frozenset([2])))
    print(operator.iconcat([1], iter([2])))

CPython (3.12.10, 3.14.4):

    [1, 2]
    [1, 2]

The C version passes both operands to [`PySequence_InPlaceConcat()`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.12.13/Objects/abstract.c#L1798-L1823), which calls the left operand's `sq_inplace_concat` or `sq_concat` without looking at the right one. It checks `PySequence_Check(o)` only on the fallback for types without those slots. The pure-Python version in [`Lib/operator.py`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.12.13/Lib/operator.py#L349-L355) checks only `a` and then runs `a += b`, so it skips the check on that fallback as well. `concat()` has the same shape ([`#L146-L151`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.12.13/Lib/operator.py#L146-L151)), though for `list` it is masked because `list + frozenset` raises anyway.

PyPy requires both operands to be sequences and raises `TypeError: 'list' object can't be concatenated` for the calls above. A PR to make PyPy match CPython (pypy/pypy#5781) was answered with "I think PyPy's behaviour is correct", reading the documented "*a* and *b* sequences" as a requirement.

So the docs and PyPy say *b* must be a sequence, while both CPython implementations accept anything the left operand's `+=` accepts. Which one is intended?

- If *b* is meant to be a sequence, the two implementations could check it, as PyPy does.

title: `ctypes.util.find_library()` searches the current working directory on macOS
body:
### Bug report

On macOS, `find_library("ssl")` returns `/usr/lib/libssl.dylib`. However, if the current working directory contains a file named `libssl.dylib` it'd return it. 

[The docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ctypes.html#finding-shared-libraries) say:

> uses the system’s standard naming schemes and paths to locate the library, and **returns a full pathname** if successful:

...and no example shows the current working directory.

On Linux current working directory doesn't have any effect.

And the cwd on macOS comes from `yield`:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/e0d0f2e153450cf79b84e2ec5ffbcbad8aea7922/Lib/ctypes/macholib/dyld.py#L99-L100

I find this behaviour surprising. If an application changes into an untrusted directory and passes the result of `find_library("ssl")` to `ctypes.CDLL()`, as in #162362, it loads the local copy.

I think `find_library()` should stop looking in the working directory. I'm more than happy to provide the PR.

CPython main branch

title: sqlite3 docs: a series of SELECTs is not a consistent read snapshot under default transaction control
body:
## Documentation gap: a series of SELECTs on one connection is not a consistent read snapshot under the default transaction control

### Summary

The docs state *which* statements implicitly open a transaction in legacy transaction-control mode, but they never state the consequence that matters in practice: **plain `SELECT`s do not start a read transaction**, so several reads on one connection (for example, exporting several tables) can observe different committed states of the database. Users commonly assume that queries issued inside one `with conn:` block form a consistent snapshot — they do not, in the default configuration.

### Environment

- Python 3.13.14, SQLite 3.53.1 (same behaviour on Python 3.14.5).
- Default `sqlite3.connect()` settings (`isolation_level=""`, `autocommit=LEGACY_TRANSACTION_CONTROL`).

### Pure-stdlib reproducer

```python
import sqlite3
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

p = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "snap.db"
c = sqlite3.connect(p)
c.execute("CREATE TABLE a (v TEXT)")
c.execute("CREATE TABLE b (v TEXT)")
c.execute("INSERT INTO a VALUES ('old')")
c.execute("INSERT INTO b VALUES ('old')")
c.commit()
c.close()

def run(isolation_level, explicit_begin):
    reader = sqlite3.connect(p, isolation_level=isolation_level)
    writer = sqlite3.connect(p, timeout=0.3)
    try:
        if explicit_begin:
            reader.execute("BEGIN")

        va = reader.execute("SELECT v FROM a").fetchone()[0]
        # another connection atomically updates BOTH tables between the two reads
        try:
            writer.execute("UPDATE a SET v='new'")
            writer.execute("UPDATE b SET v='new'")
            writer.commit()
            vb = reader.execute("SELECT v FROM b").fetchone()[0]
            result = f"a={va}, b={vb} -> {'TORN' if va != vb else 'consistent'}"
        except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
            # reader holds a shared lock => a snapshot was actually established
            result = f"a={va}; writer blocked ({e})

title: Official python:3.15-slim image segfaults on CPUs without AVX2 (3.14-slim, 3.15-bookworm and 3.15-full are fine
body:
### Crash report

The official python:3.15-slim Docker image (Debian 13/trixie, Python 3.15.2,
built with GCC 14.2.0) segfaults deterministically at interpreter startup
during import on CPUs without AVX2/BMI2/FMA.

Minimal reproducible example — on a host with an Intel Xeon E3-1220L v2
(Ivy Bridge, no avx2/bmi2/fma):

    $ docker run --rm python:3.15-slim python -c "import ctypes, ctypes.util"
    Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

    Current thread 0x0000794fe8982380 [python] (most recent call first):
      File "/usr/local/lib/python3.15/enum.py", line Segmentation fault (core dumped)

Note that simple startup still works, e.g. `python --version` and
`python -c "print(1+1)"` succeed; the crash appears once import machinery /
ctypes is exercised. In other runs the fault handler points into the import
machinery instead:

    Current thread 0x000072ace230d380 [python] (most recent call first):
      File "<frozen importlib._bootstrap>", line Segmentation fault (core dumped)

The same container image, freshly pulled and re-unpacked on a second node in
the same cluster, reproduces the crash on every start; an identical digest on
a Haswell-class node (fma bmi1 bmi2 avx2) runs cleanly. Kernel log shows the
same offset in libpython on every occurrence:

    segfault at 4 ip 00007741f0161795 sp ... error 6 in libpython3.15.so.1.0[...+299000]

CPU flag comparison between the two hosts:

    crashing host : sse4_1 sse4_2 popcnt aes avx            (Ivy Bridge, no avx2/bmi2/fma)
    working host  : fma sse4_1 sse4_2 avx bmi1 avx2 bmi2    (Haswell+)

Variants that do NOT crash on the same Ivy Bridge host:

    docker run --rm python:3.12-slim        # ok
    docker run --rm python:3.13-slim        # ok
    docker run --rm python:3.14-slim        # ok
    docker run --rm python:3.15             # full trixie build, ok
    docker run --rm python:3.15-slim-bookworm # slim build against Debian 12, glibc 2.36, ok

Variants that DO crash:

    docker run --rm python:3.15-slim

title: `mmap`: creating a file-backed map calls `fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC)` on macOS with the GIL held
body:
### Feature or enhancement

On macOS, `mmap.mmap(fd, ...)` calls `fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC)` before every file-backed mapping, even with a read-only descriptor. It holds the GIL during the call and the result gets ignored:

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/865d8d8f890352f5bb0ff58b7707179c8b046f8e/Modules/mmapmodule.c#L1881-L1892

The call was added in #55486 (buildbot crash). On a 32-bit kernel, the HFS+ function `hfs_vnop_blockmap()` truncated the remaining length of a range awaiting zero-fill to `size_t`. At 4 GiB the length wrapped to zero, so reading the mapped page raised `SIGBUS`. A full sync forced HFS+ to zero-fill the range before mapping: 

https://github.com/apple-oss-distributions/xnu/blob/161efb48ee9912c6935f205e7ac9c370edb09318/bsd/hfs/hfs_readwrite.c#L2526-L2529

I reproduced the crash on macOS 10.7.5 with the i386 kernel. Since 10.8, [macOS has used only 64-bit kernels](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Darwin/Conceptual/64bitPorting/KernelExtensionsandDrivers/KernelExtensionsandDrivers.html), where 4 GiB fits in `size_t`. And [PEP 11](https://peps.python.org/pep-0011/#support-tiers) lists only `x86_64` and `aarch64` as supported macOS targets.

### Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

No response given

### Links to previous discussion of this feature:

- #55486 (the original crash)
- #56311 ("Python should not sync the file implicitly", about a different problem)
- #56086 (`os.fsync()` and `F_FULLFSYNC`)

title: Improving the selection of bin/python symlink's target in a venv
body:
### Feature or enhancement

NOTE: The following applies only to POSIX systems and only when the `--copies` option is not given.

I'd like to propose a stricter specification of the ./bin subdirectory layout regarding the Python executable.

Three symlinks are created: `python`, `python3` and `python3.15` (using 3.15 as an example for the version being used). One of them points to the python executable installed system-wide and the remaining two point to the first one.

Unfortunately, which one points where is inconsistent:

```text
Commands and respective results in ./bin:

$ python -m venv v1

python -> /usr/bin/python
python3 -> python
python3.15 -> python

---
$ python3 -m venv v2

python -> python3
python3 -> /usr/bin/python3
python3.15 -> python3

---
$ python3.15 -m venv v3

python -> python3.15
python3 -> python3.15
python3.15 -> /usr/bin/python3.15
```

Once a year, the system-wide `/usr/bin/python` gets upgraded (say to 3.16) and that breaks all three venvs.

However, the venvs `v1` and `v2` will fail with import errors and a less experienced admin may need
more time to realize what is going on. Also `python3.15 -V` will print `3.16` which isn't OK either.

The last one (`v3`) will fail too, but with a clear error message *"command not found"*.
Another advantage is that all existing venv can be easily hot-fixed in one step by installing
the 3.15 version parallel with 3.16.

That's why the layout `v3` is preferrable and if possible it should be created regardless
of the command used to build the virtual environment.


### Has this already been discussed elsewhere?

I have already discussed this feature proposal on Discourse

### Links to previous discussion of this feature:

There were no responses on discourse:

https://discuss.python.org/t/python-symlink-target-in-virtual-envs/104800

title: zipfile.Path: __str__ and relative_to crash with TypeError when ZipFile was opened from a file-like object
body:
### Bug report

When `zipfile.Path` is constructed from an in-memory `io.BytesIO` or any file-like object (where `ZipFile.filename` is `None`), calling `str(path)` or `path.relative_to(other)` crashes with `TypeError: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not NoneType`.

#### Minimal Reproducible Example:

```python

import zipfile

# Create in-memory zip
bio = io.BytesIO()
with zipfile.ZipFile(bio, 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('a/b/c.txt', 'hello')

# Construct zipfile.Path from file-like object
root = zipfile.Path(bio)
child = root / 'a/b/c.txt'

# 1. str(child) fails
try:
    print(str(child))
except TypeError as e:
    print("str() error:", e)

# 2. relative_to fails
try:
    print(child.relative_to(root / 'a'))
except TypeError as e:
    print("relative_to() error:", e)
```

```

relative_to() error: expected str, bytes or os.PathLike object, not NoneType

title: http.cookies: SimpleCookie silently drops cookies containing standard 'Partitioned' attribute
body:
### Bug report

When parsing cookie headers with the modern `Partitioned` attribute (CHIPS / RFC 6265bis, supported across all major web browsers and modern web frameworks), `http.cookies.SimpleCookie` silently discards the entire cookie. In addition, attempting to set `morsel['partitioned'] = True` raises `CookieError: Invalid attribute 'partitioned'`.

#### Reproduction:

```python
from http import cookies

# 1. Loading a cookie with the Partitioned flag
c1 = cookies.SimpleCookie()
c1.load('session=12345; Secure; SameSite=None; Partitioned')
print('Cookies loaded (with Partitioned):', len(c1))
# Output: Cookies loaded (with Partitioned): 0  (silently dropped!)

# 2. Same cookie without Partitioned
c2 = cookies.SimpleCookie()
c2.load('session=12345; Secure; SameSite=None')
print('Cookies loaded (without Partitioned):', len(c2))
# Output: Cookies loaded (without Partitioned): 1

# 3. Attempting to set Partitioned attribute programmatically
c3 = cookies.SimpleCookie()
c3['session'] = '12345'
try:
    c3['session']['partitioned'] = True
except cookies.CookieError as e:
    print('Error setting partitioned:', e)
    # Output: Error setting partitioned: Invalid attribute 'partitioned'
```

#### Actual Behavior:
Because `'partitioned'` is not present in `Morsel._reserved` and `Morsel._flags`, when `_BaseCookie.__parse_string` encounters `Partitioned`, it hits the valueless-token fallback:
```python
            elif value is not None:
                parsed_items.append((TYPE_KEYVALUE, key, self.value_decode(value)))
                morsel_seen = True
            else:
                # Invalid cookie string
                return
```
This triggers the early `return` and causes `SimpleCookie` to discard the entire cookie header without loading any morsels.

#### Expected Behavior:
`Partitioned` should be recognized as a valid boolean flag attribute (like `Secure` and `HttpOnly`), allowing modern partitioned cookies to be parsed without dropping the cookie, and serialized

title: `__import__` too eager, make it lazy
body:
### Bug report

We have an **inconsistency**:

`import <module>` -> `ModuleType | LazyImportType`
`lazy import <module>` -> `ModuleType | LazyImportType`
`__lazy_import__(<module>)` -> `ModuleType | LazyImportType`

`importlib.import_module(<module>)` -> **`ModuleType`**
`importlib.__import__(<module>)` ->**`ModuleType`**
`__import__(<module>)` -> **`ModuleType`**

At its core, the issue seems to be that `__lazy_import__`  checks lazy filters, but `__import__` doesn't.

Consider:

```python
import sys

def my_filter(importing, imported, fromlist):
    return True

sys.set_lazy_imports_filter(my_filter)
sys.set_lazy_imports('all')

import json

print(type(globals()['json']))
```

Outputs `<class 'lazy_import'>` as expected.

But switching the `import json` to `json = __import__('json')` (or `importlib.import_module` or `importlib.__import__`) outputs `<class 'module'>`.

Not only is that inconsistent with `import` stmt, it's inconsistent with `lazy import`. Consider:

```python
import sys

def my_filter(importing, imported, fromlist):
    return False

sys.set_lazy_imports_filter(my_filter)

lazy import json

print(type(globals()['json']))
```

The output changes depending on `True` / `False` in the filter, which is intended. It also works if I switch out `lazy import json` for `json = __lazy_import__('json')`.

### CPython versions tested on:

3.15

### Operating systems tested on:

Windows

title: tkinter: os.dup2() on fds 1/2 breaks every subsequent Tcl interpreter on Windows
body:
# Bug report

### Bug description:

On Windows, once a Tcl interpreter has built its standard channels, a later `os.dup2()` onto fds 1 and 2 can make **every subsequent** `tkinter.Tk()` or `tkinter.Tcl()` fail:

```
_tkinter.TclError: Can't find a usable init.tcl in the following directories:
    {C:\Users\...\Python314\tcl\tcl8.6}

C:/Users/.../tcl/tcl8.6/init.tcl: couldn't read file "C:/Users/.../tcl/tcl8.6/init.tcl": no such file or directory
```

The file is present and readable the whole time. At the instant of the failure Python can `os.stat()` and `open()` that same path, and a Tcl interpreter created *before* the redirection can still `source` it. The errno is not real.

This is not GUI-specific — `tkinter.Tcl()` is affected too — and it does not need threads, subprocesses or a window.

### Reproducer

Fails 10/10 runs here, with stdout going to a console, a pipe, a file or `NUL`, for both `Tk()` and `Tcl()`:

```python

saved = {fd: os.dup(fd) for fd in (1, 2)}
tmp = {fd: tempfile.TemporaryFile() for fd in (1, 2)}

    if use_tcl:
        ip = tkinter.Tcl()                 # no GUI at all
        ip.eval("fconfigure stdout")       # make Tcl build its std channels
        del ip
    else:
        tkinter.Tk().destroy()

for i in range(30):
    for fd in (1, 2):                      # redirect fds 1 and 2 ...
        os.dup2(tmp[fd].fileno(), fd)
    try:
        new_interpreter()
    except Exception as exc:

        print(f"interpreter {i} failed:\n{exc}")
        sys.exit(1)
    for fd in (1, 2):                      # ... and put them back
        os.dup2(saved[fd], fd)
print("30 interpreters, no failure")
```

title: Use portable SIMD (GCC/Clang vector extensions) to speed up ASCII scanning and case conversion
body:
### Feature or enhancement

## Proposal

Several hot string routines scan or transform 1-byte data byte by byte, or at
most 8 bytes at a time with `size_t` tricks (SWAR). Examples are the ASCII
check in the UTF-8, ASCII and latin-1 decoders, `bytes.isascii()`,
`bytes.lower()`/`upper()` and the `_json` string scanner. On long inputs they
are 2-8x slower than they could be with 128-bit SIMD.

I propose adding a small, portable SIMD layer based on GCC/Clang vector
extensions (`__attribute__((vector_size(16)))`), and using it in these
routines. Every SIMD path keeps the existing scalar code as its fallback.

### Design

- **A configure check** defines `_Py_HAVE_EFFICIENT_VECTOR_EXTENSIONS` when
  both conditions hold:
  - the compiler supports 128-bit vector extensions;
  - the target has native 128-bit SIMD. That means x86-64 (SSE2, part of the
    baseline), ARM64 (NEON, part of the baseline) and ARM32 built with NEON.

  The architecture list is the same as for the existing
  `_Py_HAVE_EFFICIENT_BUILTIN_SHUFFLEVECTOR` check used by `bytes.hex()`
  (`Python/pystrhex.c`). That check is left unchanged. The new one is
  separate and more general: it doesn't need `__builtin_shufflevector`.
- **On Windows** the macro is defined for clang-cl only. MSVC doesn't support
  vector extensions, so MSVC builds keep the current code.
- **No intrinsics and no runtime CPU dispatch.** Only the baseline ISA of each
  architecture is used, so binaries stay portable. GCC and Clang emit
  SSE2/NEON from the same source (checked in the generated assembly).
- **A new internal header, `Include/internal/pycore_simd.h`,** holds the
  helpers: load, splat, "any lane non-ASCII", "any lane set", and
  `_Py_simd_skip_ascii()`, which skips ASCII-only blocks of 64 and 16 bytes.
- **The SIMD code only skips blocks that need no special handling.** The
  existing scalar code then finds the exact position. Results, error
  positions and error messages are therefore unchanged by construction, and
  the c

title: Request to restore PyWeakref_GetObject() to the v3.15 limited API
body:
### Bug report

`PyWeakref_GetObject()` was deprecated in v3.13 (when `PyWeakref_GetRef()` was added) and removed in v3.15. This means that extension modules that target older (still supported) versions cannot be built against the v3.15 headers.

#158401 shows the importance of using the latest versions of the headers where possible. Taking this issue into account v3.14 headers are the only ones that can safely be used when targeting all currently supported versions of Python.

I would like to see `PyWeakref_GetObject()` restored to the v3.15 limited API and only removed in v3.18 when it's replacement is available in all supported versions (ie. when v3.13 is the oldest supported version). If this were the case (and the principle followed for other similar situations) then extension authors could always build using the latest supported headers.

title: Add debug assert for out-of-bounds dk_indices values in do_lookup
body:
### Bug report

`_Py_dict_lookup` in `Objects/dictobject.c` validates `dk_indices` values with `ix >= 0` but does not assert `ix < dk->dk_nentries`. When `dk_indices` contains a stale or corrupted index (e.g. from a dict-watcher callback that mutates the dict during `_PyDict_NotifyEvent`, violating the "must not modify" contract), `do_lookup` silently reads past the `dk_entries` array.

Adding a debug-mode assert would catch this class of API misuse early instead of producing a delayed, hard-to-diagnose crash.

Suggested one-line fix in `_Py_dict_lookup`, after computing `ix` from `dk_indices`:

```c
assert(ix < dk->dk_nentries);
```

This was suggested by @encukou in GHSA-mrcp-4g4x-xg9v as a public hardening improvement.

title: Optimising sparse dict copy
body:
### Feature or enhancement

Currently when cloning a dict and it's sparse (less than 30% used keys) we fallback to standard un optimised `dict_merge` even though it would have passed the other optimising enabling checks.

```
           (1) type(mp) doesn't override tp_iter; and
           (2) 'mp' is not a split-dict; and
           (3) if 'mp' is non-compact ('del' operation does not resize dicts),
               do fast-copy only if it has at most 1/3 non-used keys.
```

A "fast" sparse dict copy would involve allocating a new dict of the source sparse size and then iterating source and copying the key, values where they are set rather than going through the generic insertion code path.

From some benchmarks this can lead up to a 4x speedup, although for more common cases this is at 2x.

  | Case | main | main + sparse_copy | Speedup | Peak memory (both builds) |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          
  |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           
  | `copy()`, compact, 4 keys | 26 ns | 26 ns | 1.0x | - |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  | `copy()`, compact, 300 str keys | 350 ns | 353 ns | 1.0x | - |

title: mimetypes: reading the Windows registry through HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT is slow
body:
### Feature or enhancement

On Windows the first `mimetypes` lookup calls `_winapi._mimetypes_read_windows_registry`, which enumerates every subkey of `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT` and opens each `.ext` key through it. Since gh-159428 the registry is the only default source on Windows, so every process that guesses a type pays for it.

On a Windows 11 26100 developer machine (5,788 subkeys under HKCR, 976 extension keys, 414 with a `Content Type`), `python -c "import mimetypes; mimetypes.init()"` costs 75 ms more than `python -c pass` (on Linux, 3 ms). Most of it is opening keys through the merged view, about 60 µs each. Opening the same keys in `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes` and `HKCU\Software\Classes` directly is several times cheaper:

| reading | ms |
|---|---:|
| current: enumerate HKCR, open each `.ext` key through HKCR | 80-113 |
| HKLM classes then HKCU classes, open each `.ext` key in its own hive | 43-51 |

I changed the C reader to walk `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes` and then `HKCU\Software\Classes` (HKCU second, so its values win) and timed `mimetypes.init()` with the same 3.14.4 build otherwise: 32.6 ms faster [29.5, 37.9], 40 interleaved runs.

To give exactly the same result as HKCR, the two lists need merging, which costs nothing next to the registry calls:

- a value missing under an HKCU key falls back to HKLM (129 extensions here exist in HKCU without `Content Type`);
- HKCR spells the key as HKCU does (`.aac` in HKCU, `.AAC` in HKLM);
- HKCR enumerates in sorted order.

The pure-Python fallback `MimeTypes._read_windows_registry` would change the same way, so that `test_registry_accelerator` keeps comparing like with like. It currently opens every HKCR subkey, not just the extensions, before checking the name, which could be fixed in passing.

Does this sound reasonable? I can prepare a PR with the merged per-hive reader for both implementations.

title: Windows venv python.exe starts a second process; could the launcher run the interpreter in-process?
body:
### Feature or enhancement

On Windows, `Scripts\python.exe` in a venv is `venvlauncher.exe`. It reads `pyvenv.cfg`, starts the base `python.exe` as a child process and waits for it (bpo-34977). On Linux and macOS the venv's `python` is a symlink, so there is one process.

The second process costs about 16 ms on every start. `python -c pass` with python-build-standalone 3.14.4 on an i9-10900K, Windows 11 26100, 40-60 interleaved runs, paired 95% intervals:

| | ms |
|---|---:|
| base `python.exe` | 35-40 |
| venv `python.exe` (launcher), minus base | +16.2 [14.4, 16.7], +17.1 [16.0, 17.9] (two runs) |
| venv created with `--symlinks`, minus base | +3.4 to +4.5 |
| Linux venv minus Linux base | +0.3 |

Most tools run Python through a venv (`.venv\Scripts\python.exe`, `uv run`, IDEs, test runners), so this is paid on nearly every call. `uv venv` copies the same launcher, so it has the same cost.

I tried a launcher that does the same lookup and then loads the base interpreter into its own process:

1. read `home` from `pyvenv.cfg`, as `venvlauncher.c` does;
2. `AddDllDirectory(home)`, so extension modules still resolve `python3.dll`;
3. `LoadLibraryExW(home\python3XY.dll, LOAD_WITH_ALTERED_SEARCH_PATH)` and call `Py_Main(argc, argv)`.

getpath then finds `pyvenv.cfg` next to the executable, as it does for a symlinked `python.exe`. With that launcher, `sys.executable`, `sys.prefix`, `sys.base_prefix`, `sys._base_executable` and `sys.path` are the same as with the current launcher, a `spawn` multiprocessing pool and a `subprocess` child of `sys.executable` work, and extension modules (`_ssl`, `_ctypes`, `sqlite3`) load. Start-up becomes the same as the base interpreter: +0.6 ms [−0.8, +2.5], 16.1 ms [14.1, 17.2] less than the current launcher.

title: configparser: write() silently drops leading whitespace from multiline values on round-trip
body:
### Bug report

If a value contains a newline followed by whitespace, writing and reading it back silently loses the whitespace with no error.

```python
import configparser, io

c = configparser.ConfigParser()
c['s'] = {'k': 'line1\n\tline2'}

buf = io.StringIO()
c.write(buf)

c2 = configparser.ConfigParser()
c2.read_string(buf.getvalue())
print(repr(c2['s']['k']))
# Got:      'line1\nline2'
# Expected: 'line1\n\tline2'
```

The written file has:
```
[s]
k = line1
line2
```

`_write_section` adds `\n\t` to mark continuation lines. On read, `_handle_continuation_line` calls `.strip()` on each line — which strips both the added tab AND any whitespace that was part of the original value.

On 3.14+, `write()` should raise `InvalidWriteError` here, same as it already does for keys with leading whitespace (gh-96239). On earlier versions the data is just silently lost.

### CPython versions tested on:

3.13+

### Operating systems tested on:

Linux

body:
### What kind of issue is this? - [x] React Compiler core (the JS output is incorrect, or your app works incorrectly after optimization) - [ ] babel-plugin-react-compiler (build issue installing or using the Babel plugin) - [ ] eslint-plugin-react-hooks (build issue installing or using the eslint plugin) - [ ] react-compiler-healthcheck (build issue installing or using the healthcheck script) ### Link to repro https://playground.react.dev/#N4Igzg9grgTgxgUxALhAMygOzgFwJYSYAEAggA5kAUAlEcADrFEbb6FEC2AhgNYIASXTABMANghg06jIrKIwEOWMSkBeAHxEAjAG4ZRAL764hMDiJciqzrwFCxEmnqYnMZogCMrNvoJHjJamdZLgA6HC4Ac296dDwYM1jg+UVlIgAeMnVgAGUcGDxMSMpLVTLPagM6PIKiyg9wqMr0gHos5yNMEAAaEFc0PEiUEAYmFpaTDjI8US42TABZCGEEZCJYrlFRWMYDHvAACwgAdwBJTBwJTE2wFDQbhAMgA ### Repro steps A capture-free arrow inside a helper function is outlined to module scope, so each call of the helper returns the same `_temp` instead of a new function. ```jsx function App() { function makeHandler() { return () => 1; } const a = makeHandler(); const b = makeHandler(); a.tag = "first"; return

{String(a === b)} {String(b.tag)}

; } ``` Render `` with `renderToStaticMarkup`. Expected (without the compiler): `

false undefined

` Actual (with the compiler): `

true first

` `makeHandler` compiles to `return _temp;` with `function _temp() { return 1; }` at module level, so the function (and anything set on it) is also shared across renders and component instances. No diagnostic is reported for `a.tag = "first"` even with `panicThreshold: "all_errors"`. Outlining arrows written directly in the component body seems fine (#33138); the problem is outlining inside a function that can run more than once per render. ### How often does this bug happen? Every time ### What version of React are you using? 19.3.1 ### What version of React Compiler are you using? 1.0.0 (also main at 2363bc2) Credit: https://ucsbplse.github.io/

title: [Compiler Bug]: `obj.x++` on a member is compiled to `obj.x = obj.x + 1`, so numeric strings are concatenated
[Compiler Bug]: Assignment to computed member evaluates RHS constant before key update
body:
### What kind of issue is this? - [x] React Compiler core (the JS output is incorrect, or your app works incorrectly after optimization) - [ ] babel-plugin-react-compiler (build issue installing or using the Babel plugin) - [ ] eslint-plugin-react-hooks (build issue installing or using the eslint plugin) - [ ] react-compiler-healthcheck (build issue installing or using the healthcheck script) ### Link to repro https://gist.github.com/trackoor/7e59f5d01b0c39cf84549fa41c0c9564 ### Repro steps 1. Compile the following component with `babel-plugin-react-compiler`: ```jsx function App() { const a = [0, 0]; let i = 0; a[i++] = i; return

{a.join(",")}

; } ``` 2. Render ``. **Expected behavior:** Uncompiled JavaScript evaluates the left-hand side reference `a[i++]` before reading the right-hand side `i`, updating `i` to `1` so `App` renders `

1,0

`. **Actual behavior:** With React Compiler, the component renders `

0,0

` because the assignment is compiled to: ```js a = [0, 0]; a[0] = 0; ``` During HIR lowering of `AssignmentExpression` with `=`, the right-hand side is lowered before the left-hand side `MemberExpression`, so constant propagation resolves the right-hand side `i` to `0` before `i++` takes effect. Credit: https://ucsbplse.github.io/ ### How often does this bug happen? Every time ### What version of React are you using? 19.3.1 ### What version of React Compiler are you using? 1.0.0

title: Bug: dev-mode Component Performance Track prop diff re-walks aliased references; cost scales linearly with alias count
body:
## Summary

In development builds, the Component Performance Track's prop diff (`addObjectDiffToProperties` / `addValueToProperties`) keeps no record of objects it has already visited. When one prop object exposes the same underlying data under several names — a common shape in data-table and ORM-style libraries — the walk repeats in full for each name.

Cost scales **linearly with the number of aliases**, even though the aliases add no new objects. Measured below: ~120 entries per alias name, for the same array reference.

The effect is multiplied by component count, because the diff runs per component render. In a real application this rendered a page unresponsive for 83% of sampled checks over 15 minutes, at ~1.9M entries/second sustained. Production is unaffected, as documented.

## Relationship to #34770 / #34803

This is not a re-report of #34770. That issue described **memory growth** from the same functions and was closed by #34803, which adds `performance.clearMeasures()`.

That fix is present in the build measured here — verified by fingerprint rather than version string: `clearMeasures` present (8 occurrences), #34803's own typo correction present (`reusableChangedPropsEntry`, 2 occurrences) with zero occurrences of the pre-fix spelling.

`clearMeasures` bounds **retention**. It does not bound **production**: the walk still runs in full and still allocates every entry before `measure()` is called. The behavior reported here is the cost of producing the entries, not of keeping them.

## Reproduction

Self-contained. Renders 20 components, each receiving one object that exposes the same 25-row array under N names, re-created every 250ms. Counts entries via `PerformanceObserver` — no React patching, since `detail` is structured-cloned at `measure()` time.

```jsx
'use client';
import React, { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';

const NAMES = ['rows','flatRows','rowsById','preGroupedRows','groupedRows','preSortedRows',
  'sortedRows','preFilteredRows

processStringChunk accepts the content chunk and resolves the text row as "x", even though a one-code-unit JavaScript string cannot have a UTF-8 byte length of 4096.

rowLength < chunk.length
```

title: Bug: acquireSingletonInstance removes all attributes when a Host Singleton remounts
body:
Remounting a Host Singleton (`<html>`, `<head>`, `<body>`) removes **every** attribute from that DOM node, including attributes React never rendered. `acquireSingletonInstance` clears the node and then reinitialises it from props, so an attribute written by a pre-hydration inline script is destroyed. I hit this in an app with a dark-mode toggle plus a language switcher: switching language remounts `<html>`, and the `data-theme` written by the theme script is gone. For the common `localStorage` / `prefers-color-scheme` FOUC script the attribute cannot be a React prop at first paint, because it has to be set before React exists on the page. (A cookie-based theme can be a prop, at the cost of opting the route out of static rendering.)

Hydration does not take this path, so a plain page load is correct and only a later remount loses the attribute. Whichever behaviour is intended, the two paths disagree.

This is **not** fixed by #37112: that PR changed `releaseSingletonInstance` only. `acquireSingletonInstance` is unchanged on `main` and still loops `removeAttributeNode` over every attribute. #37112 added a gated `// @gate TODO` test for the acquire path covering the cold acquire (`createRoot` over a node that already had an attribute); this report is the remount entry into the same function, reachable from a stock app with no imperative setup. It still reproduces on a canary that contains #37112, which isolates acquire as the remaining cause.

React version: 19.2.8 (also reproduced on 19.3.0-canary-96fcba90-20260728). Not a regression as far as I can tell — the loop is present in shipped 19.2.8 and Host Singletons are 19-only.

## Summary

Since React 19.2's batched Suspense reveal ("Batching Suspense Boundaries for SSR streaming"), the inline `completeBoundary` runtime (`$RC`) no longer consumes its content segment synchronously — it queues `(boundary, content)` pairs into `$RB` and consumes them in a deferred `revealCompletedBoundaries` (`$RV`) flush (rAF, then a ~300ms/2.3s-LCP throttle). The queued content segment `<div hidden id="S:n">` therefore **stays in the DOM with its id until the flush**.

In a prerender+resume (PPR) document, the resume stream's segment ids are allocated independently of the prerender's, so a resume segment can legally reuse an id the shell already used for a boundary completion — one document containing two `<div hidden id="S:4">` (the shell boundary `B:4`'s completion segment, and the resume segment feeding postponed hole `P:4` via `$RS("S:4","P:4")`). This was safe pre-19.2 **by ordering**: each segment was consumed and removed synchronously by its own inline script before the next same-id segment parsed.

With batching, when the whole document is parsed in one burst (CDN cache hit / fast network / busy main thread delaying rAF), the parser executes `$RS("S:4","P:4")` while the shell's `S:4` is still queued and in the DOM. `completeSegment`'s `document.getElementById("S:4")` returns the **first (wrong) segment** and moves the wrong subtree into the resume hole. The subsequent `$RV` flush then operates on a cross-linked tree and throws:

```
HierarchyRequestError: Failed to execute 'insertBefore' on 'Node': The new child element contains the parent.
```

leaving orphaned never-consumed hidden segments, after which hydration fails (`Minified React error #418` storm — observed 7–38 per load) and React discards the SSR output and client-renders. In the worst observed case the boundary's fallback had already been deleted when the insert threw, leaving a blank region and a pegged main thread (user-facing "Page Unresponsive").

## Environment

- react-dom `19.2.3`

[Flight] Let encodeFormAction reuse the default encoding
body:
## Summary

This is a follow-up to #27563.

The SSR Flight client's `encodeFormAction` callback fully replaces React's default form action encoding. A framework cannot call the default encoder and change only one field.

A common use case is changing the form action URL while keeping the default encoding, so `decodeAction` still works. For example, a framework may add a query parameter that identifies a no-JS action request without reading the request body.

Today, frameworks must copy React's encoding behavior using public APIs. This includes serializing the arguments, renaming fields, generating prefixes, caching results, and handling suspension. The callback also does not receive `identifierPrefix` or a stable identity for unbound references.

This logic now exists in two implementations:

* waku: https://github.com/wakujs/waku/pull/2191
* `@vitejs/plugin-rsc`: https://github.com/vitejs/vite-plugin-react/pull/1280

## Proposal

Pass a bound default encoder to the callback:

```ts
encodeFormAction?: (
  id: string,
  args: Promise<unknown[]>,
  encodeDefault: () => ReactCustomFormAction,
) => ReactCustomFormAction;
```

A framework could then write:

```ts
const encodeFormAction = (id, args, encodeDefault) => ({
  ...encodeDefault(),
  action: currentUrl + '?my-marker=1',
});
```

React would keep control of caching, prefixes, and suspension, while frameworks could change only the fields they need.

Exporting `defaultEncodeFormAction` would not solve this by itself because React must bind the reference state and provide the Fizz `identifierPrefix`.

## `useActionState` permalink

When `permalink` is set, Fizz applies it after `encodeFormAction` and replaces the callback's action URL.

Applying the permalink before the callback, or adding a final action transform, would let frameworks preserve their URL changes.

title: Build: Inject the runtime React version from ReactVersions.js
body:
## Summary

Use `ReactVersions.js` as the single source of truth for React's runtime version and inject that value during the build.

## Current behavior

`packages/shared/ReactVersion.js` currently hard-codes the React version:

```js
export default '19.3.0';
```

The file contains a TODO explaining that the version should instead be injected during the build from `ReactVersions.js`.

This creates multiple version values that must be updated together, including:

- `ReactVersions.js`
- `packages/shared/ReactVersion.js`
- Package metadata such as `packages/react/package.json`

A missed update could cause runtime version information, release metadata, and DevTools compatibility handling to disagree.

## Proposed change

1. Add a build-time version token or equivalent injection mechanism.
2. Source the injected value from `ReactVersions.js`.
3. Update `packages/shared/ReactVersion.js` to use the injected value, or remove the module if its consumers can be migrated safely.
4. Ensure source-mode tests and local development receive a deterministic version.
5. Cover stable, canary, and experimental release channels.
6. Add validation that detects divergence between emitted runtime metadata and canonical release metadata.

The existing Rollup constant replacement stage in `scripts/rollup/build.js` may provide a suitable integration point.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ReactVersions.js` is the only manually maintained source for the core React release version.
- Stable builds expose the canonical React version at runtime.
- Canary and experimental builds expose their expected release-channel version formats.
- Source tests, watch builds, production builds, and release builds do not contain an unresolved version token.
- DevTools version compatibility behavior continues to work.
- CI reports a clear failure if runtime and canonical release metadata diverge.
- The obsolete TODO and duplicate runtime version constant are removed.

title: Transient DOM duplication window (~300 ms) when batched Suspense reveal races hydration-time client render of dehydrated boundaries (React 19.2)
body:
**Summary**

Since React 19.2, two documented behaviors interact to produce a transient window where
streamed Suspense content exists twice in the DOM:

1. **Batched/throttled Suspense reveals** (React 19.2 blog): when `$RC(...)` executes for a
   streamed segment, the reveal may be queued for ~300 ms instead of applying immediately.
2. **Client-rendering dehydrated boundaries on document load** (#31620): if the
   document finishes loading and hydration finds a Suspense boundary still "dehydrated
   pending", React client-renders it from the flight payload.

When both fire on the same boundary — reveal queued at t≈75 ms, document load + hydration at
t≈100 ms — the client render mounts a **visible** copy while the streamed segment
(`<div hidden id="S:0">…`) remains unconsumed in the DOM. Both copies coexist until the queued
reveal batch runs (~300 ms after `$RC`), finds the boundary already resolved, and deletes the
orphaned segments.

**Impact**

- End users: none observed — the extra copy is `hidden` (excluded from the accessibility
  tree) and self-cleans within ~300 ms.
- Tooling: any DOM-wide query during the window sees duplicates. Playwright strict-mode
  aborts immediately on the violation (no retry), producing persistent flaky failures for
  any assertion issued right after `page.goto()` to a streamed route. This bit us across
  ~27 spec files until we adopted `.filter({ visible: true })` everywhere (the mitigation
  the Next.js team recommends in vercel/next.js#86577 for the Activity/cacheComponents
  variant — which we do NOT use; our app has neither).

**Reproduction (deterministic, production build)**

Environment: Next.js 16.2.x (App Router), React 19.2.x, a route with `loading.tsx` whose RSC
payload streams after the shell (any data-bound page works).

1. `next build && next start`.
2. Warm the server (visit the route once) — a warm server makes hydration consistently win

title: [Tool] Structural duplicates in React codebase (34.1% of .ts/.tsx files affected)
body:
## Structural duplicates in React codebase (34.1% of .ts/.tsx files affected)

I ran [find-duplicates](https://github.com/DecSec2030/find-duplicates) — a tool that detects structural code duplicates (normalizing identifiers, strings, and whitespace before comparing) — on the main branch at `c0c39a6`.

### Summary

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| .ts/.tsx files scanned | 521 |
| Files with duplicates | 178 (34.1%) |
| Duplicate groups | 342 |
| Duplicated blocks | 973 |

### By directory

| Directory | Duplicates | Files |
|-----------|-----------|-------|
| `compiler/packages/` | 816 | 165 |
| `packages/eslint-plugin-react-hooks/` | 85 | 6 |
| `compiler/scripts/` | 64 | 5 |
| `packages/react/` | 6 | 1 |
| `fixtures/` | 2 | 1 |

### Notable findings

**1. `compiler/packages/snap/src/minimize.ts` — 30 near-identical generator methods (142 duplicates)**

Functions like `removeStatements`, `removeCallArguments`, `removeFunctionParameters`, `simplifyCallExpressions`, etc. all follow the exact same pattern: count AST nodes of a type → loop with clone → traverse → replace. This is the single largest source of duplication.

**2. `compiler/scripts/ts-compile-fixture.ts` — 14 identical pipeline passes (64 duplicates)**

Each pipeline pass checks `if (env.hasErrors()) { return formatEnvError(...); }` with near-identical structure across all passes.

**3. `compiler/packages/babel-plugin-react-compiler/` — scattered scope/binding checks (15 files)**

A pattern of checking bindings and scope ranges (`if (binding) { ... }`) is repeated across 15 different files in the compiler, suggesting a candidate for a shared utility.

**4. Core `packages/react/` is clean — only 6 duplicate blocks in 1 file.**

The mature React core has very few structural duplicates, which is expected for a well-refactored codebase.

### Context

The vast majority of duplicates are in `compiler/` (React Forget), a newer, actively-developed package. The core React packages are essentially clean.

title: Bug: [Fizz] Suspense completion instruction ($RC) emitted twice when a suspended fallback outlives completed content (19.2.x; fixed on main, needs backport)
body:
React version: 19.2.7 (all of 19.2.0 – 19.2.7; not present in 19.1.1; already fixed on main — see "Versions" below)

## Summary

In react-dom **19.2.0 through 19.2.7**, `renderToPipeableStream` emits the completion instruction for the same Suspense boundary **twice** when all of the following hold:

1. the boundary's `fallback` itself suspends at its root (e.g. an async component as the fallback element), and
2. the boundary's content also suspends but **completes while the fallback is still pending**, after the boundary's placeholder has been flushed, and
3. the content is larger than 500 bytes (`isEligibleForOutlining`).

Depending on flush interleaving the stream contains either a literal duplicate `$RC("B:n","S:n")`, or a late fallback segment that re-declares the already-revealed boundary as a fresh `<!--$?--><template id="B:m">` followed by a second `$RC("B:m","S:m")` (plus a `$RS` whose target placeholder was already consumed by the first reveal). In both cases the client-side instructions reference DOM that no longer exists; React recovers by client rendering and logs **error #419** for the boundary.

Real-world impact: Next.js 15 App Router apps vendor the 19.2 line, so a route `loading.tsx` or `<Suspense fallback>` that accidentally contains an async server component hits #419 on every **warm** production render — content resolves fast from caches while the async fallback still yields a task, which is exactly the trigger timing. We debugged this from a production regression where a shared app-shell component gained an `await` and every warm render of the affected routes started failing hydration.

Bug: ViewTransition fails to animate shared elements inside RTL layouts
body:
When using React's `ViewTransition` component in a Next.js application, shared element transitions do not work if the document or any ancestor element has `dir="rtl"`.

The exact same code works correctly when `dir="ltr"` is used.

As a workaround, wrapping the transition element in an ancestor with `dir="ltr"` restores the expected behavior.

React version:

* react: 19.2.0
* react-dom: 19.2.0
* next: 16.2.9

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Create a Next.js application using React 19 and enable View Transitions.
2. Set `<html dir="rtl">` in the root layout.
3. Create two pages with a shared `<ViewTransition name="box">`.
4. Navigate between the pages.
5. Observe that no shared element transition occurs.
6. Change `dir="rtl"` to `dir="ltr"` and repeat the navigation.

<!--
  Your bug will get fixed much faster if we can run your code and it doesn't
  have dependencies other than React. Issues without reproduction steps or
  code examples may be immediately closed as not actionable.
-->

Link to code example:

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
export default function RootLayout({
  children,
}: {
  children: React.ReactNode;
}) {
  return (
    <html dir="rtl">
      <body>{children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

## The current behavior

No shared element transition animation is performed when navigating between pages while `dir="rtl"` is applied. The navigation happens immediately without any transition.

## The expected behavior

Shared element transitions should work regardless of the text direction (`ltr` or `rtl`) applied to the document or ancestor elements.

title: Bug: [DevMode] React Flight RSC dev async-debug tracking retains unbounded ancestry in pendingOperations under   long-lived async workloads
body:
Summary

  While investigating repeated development-server memory restarts in a Next.js 16.2.9 + React 19.2.x app, I
  traced the retained memory to React Flight's development-only async-debug tracking in
  react-server-dom-turbopack-server.

  Heap snapshots show a bounded number of live pendingOperations entries retaining a much larger, growing
  ancestry graph through .previous / .awaited / .promise (WeakRef) links. A long-lived async context (e.g. an
  open stream / keepalive doing periodic awaited work) keeps the tail of an ancestry chain alive, which
  transitively pins the entire lineage. The retained graph grows without bound for the lifetime of the context.

  This does not occur in production builds (the tracking is *.development.js-only).

  I want to keep the claim narrow: React's dev async-ancestry tracking appears to retain unbounded lineage under
  long-lived async workloads — not "React has a memory leak."

  Environment

  - react-server-dom-turbopack 19.2.7 (bundled by Next.js 16.2.9), and reproduces on latest canary
  19.3.0-canary-e92ecef2-20260618 (the four async-hook callbacks are byte-for-byte identical between the two).
  - Node v22.21.1
  - Development mode only (NODE_ENV !== 'production')
  - The tracking is installed unconditionally via async_hooks.createHook({...}).enable() in
  react-server-dom-turbopack-server.node.development.js.

  Observed behavior

  A long-lived async workload causes retained ancestry to grow continuously even though the number of live
  operations stays bounded.

  From one captured in-flight heap snapshot of the dev server:
  - pendingOperations Map: ~20,377 live entries
  - Retained ancestry reachable from it: ~1.5M nodes (~1.25M objects via .awaited, ~842K via .previous, ~1.5M
  WeakRef)
  - Path-to-root of a sampled WeakRef:
  WeakRef ←promise← Object ←previous← Object ←previous← … (deep .previous chain) …

React version: 19.1.0-canary (Latest main branch)

There is a memory leak vulnerability in the React DOM Fizz Server (`ReactDOMFizzServerNode.js`) when utilizing `renderToReadableStream` and `resume` for web streams. Currently, when an `AbortSignal` is passed through options, an event listener is attached to the signal to abort the stream request if necessary. 

However, when the stream completes successfully or terminates due to an error, the `abortListener` is never cleared. This keeps a reference to the request context and stream handlers alive in memory, preventing garbage collection on long-lived `AbortSignal` references.

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Pass a shared or long-lived `AbortSignal` into `renderToReadableStream` options across multiple SSR requests.
2. Observe that every single request appends a new listener to the signal that stays attached indefinitely even after the stream is fully closed or finished.
3. This leads to a continuous build-up of memory under heavy traffic, causing a severe memory leak in Node.js/Edge environments.

title: Bug: React.lazy waits ~300ms before rendering even when the preloaded promise has resolved
body:
React version: 19.2.6

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Open the repro repository: https://github.com/andyzhan7/react-suspense-fallback-throttle

2. Open either reproduction file:
   - `precreated-routes.html`
   - `render-created-loader.html`

3. Wait until the `Student` and `Teacher` loaders have been preloaded.

4. Click `Student` or `Teacher`.

Link to code example: https://github.com/andyzhan7/react-suspense-fallback-throttle

## The current behavior

A route component loaded through `React.lazy` can be delayed by about 300ms on its first render, even when the loader promise has already resolved before that render.

The repro uses this minimal lazy route wrapper:

```js
function LazyLoader(loader) {
  const Comp = React.lazy(loader)
  return props => React.createElement(
    React.Suspense,
    null,
    React.createElement(Comp, props || null),
  )
}
```

The route loaders are preloaded on page load. They simulate network/chunk loading with a short `sleep(...)`, so by the time the user clicks `Student` or `Teacher`, the loader promise has already resolved.

However, the first render of the lazy route still commits about 300ms later:

```text
0.5ms loader called: Student
302.1ms content committed: Student
```

Because the Suspense boundary has no fallback, this appears as a blank content area for about 300ms.

## The expected behavior

If a `React.lazy` loader promise has already resolved, React should render the loaded component as soon as that resolved promise is observed, instead of waiting for the 300ms fallback throttle window.

In this case, after clicking `Student` or `Teacher`, the route content should commit immediately or near-immediately because the lazy loader promise was already resolved by preload.

Bug: `useEffect` infinite loops are silent in production - `NESTED_PASSIVE_UPDATE_LIMIT` check is `__DEV__`-only and never throws
body:
Infinite render loop detection silently degrades in production - `useEffect` loops never throw, never trigger error boundaries, and are invisible to error monitoring tools. There are two related problems in `throwIfInfiniteUpdateLoopDetected` (`ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`): **A)** The `NESTED_PASSIVE_UPDATE_LIMIT` guard (passive effects / `useEffect`) is wrapped entirely in `if (__DEV__)`. In production it does not exist at all the loop runs forever with no throw, no error boundary trigger, and no signal to `onUncaughtError`. **B)** The newer `enableInfiniteRenderLoopDetection` instrumentation path for synchronous lanes (`NESTED_UPDATE_SYNC_LANE` / `NESTED_UPDATE_PHASE_SPAWN`) also falls back to `else if (__DEV__) { console.error(...) }` when `enableInfiniteRenderLoopDetectionForceThrow` is `false`. This makes the new path *weaker* than the legacy path it sits alongside, which unconditionally throws in production. title: Bug: Remove Synthetic Events
Bug: `react-is@19` does not recognise elements from React 18
body:
React version: 18.3.1 / 19.2.5 (both affected)

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Install `react@18` and `react@19` alongside `react-is@19` (using npm package aliases)
2. Create an element with each React version
3. Call `isElement()` from `react-is@19` on each element

Link to code example: https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/f4ch33

## The current behavior

`react-is@19` returns `false` for elements created by React 17/18.

React 19 changed `$$typeof` from `Symbol(react.element)` to `Symbol(react.transitional.element)`. `react-is@19` only checks for the new symbol and does not recognise the old one.

```
react-is@19 .isElement() on react@19 element: true
react-is@19 .isElement() on react@18 element: false  ← broken
```

This breaks any tool that upgrades to `react-is@19` while its users are still on React 17/18. We hit this in [jestjs/jest#15402](https://github.com/jestjs/jest/issues/15402) - `pretty-format`'s `ReactElement` plugin silently falls back to printing elements as plain objects.

## The expected behavior

`react-is@19` should recognise elements created by React 17 and 18. Alternative is what I do in https://github.com/jestjs/jest/pull/16123 (use both `react-is@18` _and_ `react-is@19`) but that feels like an unnecessary burden to place on the community

(Disclaimer - Claude Code wrote the reproduction and this OP 😀)

title: Bug: `<style precedence>` resources permanently lost when portal container is removed from DOM
body:
When a `createPortal` container holds `<style precedence>` elements and is later removed from the DOM, React's `hoistableStyles` map keeps references to the destroyed `<style>` nodes and never re-creates them. Any component depending on those styles loses them for the rest of the session, even rendering in a connected tree.

React version: `19.0.0` through `19.2.5`, and canary `19.3.0-canary-ad5dfc82-20260427`

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Render a component using `<style href="x" precedence="custom">` inside a `createPortal` whose container is a detached div
2. Render the same component (same href) directly in the main tree
3. Remove the portal container from the DOM
4. The directly-rendered component loses its styles and never gets them back

Link to code example: https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-fkhvowjt

## The current behavior
React inserts the `<style>` into the portal container because `getRootNode()` on a detached element returns itself. When a second instance of the same resource renders in the main tree, React sees the existing `hoistableStyles` entry and reuses it, but the actual element still lives inside the portal container. Removing that container destroys the `<style>` node. The map still points to the dead node (`isConnected: false, parentNode: DIV`), so React never re-creates it. Styles are gone.

## The expected behavior
Removing a portal container should not destroy style resources used by components elsewhere in the tree. `acquireResource` should check whether a cached style instance is still connected and re-create it if not.

title: Improvement: useEffect/useInsertionEffect/useLayoutEffect null-check warning messages are vague and don't distinguish null vs undefined
body:
## Summary

The dev-mode `console.warn` messages for `useEffect`, `useInsertionEffect`, and `useLayoutEffect` in `packages/react/src/ReactHooks.js` are currently vague when the `create` callback is `null` or `undefined`.

## Current Behavior

All three hooks produce this generic message:

```
React Hook useEffect requires an effect callback. Did you forget to pass a callback to the hook?
```

This message:
- Does **not** distinguish between `null` and `undefined` being passed
- Does **not** explain what the callback signature should look like
- Leaves beginners confused about what the correct fix is

## Expected Behavior

The warning should:
1. Say explicitly whether `null` or `undefined` was received
2. Explain that the hook expects a function that optionally returns a cleanup function
3. Be consistent across all three effect hooks

**Example improved message:**
```
React Hook useEffect received a null effect callback. useEffect must be passed a function that optionally returns a cleanup function. Did you accidentally pass nothing or the result of a function call instead of the function itself?
```

## Motivation

This is a very common beginner mistake — for example, passing `useEffect(someAsyncFn(), [])` (calling the function) instead of `useEffect(someAsyncFn, [])` (passing the function). A clearer error message would surface the root cause faster.

## Fix

A fix has been submitted in PR #36361.

## Affected Files

- `packages/react/src/ReactHooks.js`

title: Bug: useOptimistic fails to revert when independent async actions overlap due to global scope entanglement
body:
There is a correctness bug in useOptimistic where the "revert" mechanism is gated by a global (per-root) async action reference count rather than being scoped to the specific action or transition that triggered it.

In an application where two unrelated components trigger async actions, a "Slow" action in Component A will prevent the optimistic UI in Component B from reverting or finalizing, even after Component B's action has fully resolved or failed.

### The Root Cause
The issue is located in ReactFiberAsyncAction.js. The implementation currently uses module-level variables to track the state of "entangled" actions:

**// From ReactFiberAsyncAction.js**
let currentEntangledPendingCount: number = 0;
let currentEntangledListeners: Array<() => mixed> | null = null;

As noted in the source comments, React currently entangles all concurrent async actions because it lacks a mechanism like AsyncContext to distinguish between them. While this entanglement might be an intentional trade-off for scheduling, it breaks the functional requirements of useOptimistic. Specifically, pingEngtangledActionScope only notifies listeners (which useOptimistic relies on) when the global currentEntangledPendingCount returns to zero

### Reproduction
I have verified this behavior in a Vite-based React environment.
https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/frosty-https-d46684

Bug: Optimize shallowEqual to avoid allocating keysB array
body:
shallowEqual() is called on every render cycle by React.memo and PureComponent.shouldComponentUpdate. In the current implementation, Object.keys(objB) allocates a full heap array that is used only to read its .length property, then is immediately discarded as garbage.

**Current Problem:**

```const keysA = Object.keys(objA);  // needed — iterated below
  const keysB = Object.keys(objB);  // ONLY .length is ever read
  //            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ allocates a throw-away array

  if (keysA.length !== keysB.length) {
    return false;
  }
```

**Proposed change**
Replace Object.keys(objB) with an inline own-property counter using for...in + hasOwnProperty. This:

1.   Avoids the heap allocation of the keysB array entirely.
2.   Adds an early-exit: returns false the moment objB's own key count exceeds keysA.length, without enumerating the rest.
3.   Is behaviourally identical in ALL cases, same output for every possible input (null-prototype objects, symbol keys, inherited enumerable properties all handled correctly).

**Benchmark (Node 22, 10 million iterations)**

  Scenario                                        Before                After                     Gain
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Equal objects, 5 keys                     312 ms              248 ms                 +20%
  Different key count (3 vs 5)           198 ms             134 ms                  +32%
  Single-key objects                         145 ms             119 ms                  +18%
  Equal objects, 20 keys                    891 ms            743 ms                  +16%

Full reproducible benchmark script will be in the PR.

I willing to submit a PR, including full tests, benchmark script, and Flow types.

title: [React Compiler Bug] `&&` conditional renders `0` as text node when first operand is falsy
body:
## Bug Description When using the `A && B && C && ` conditional rendering pattern, if the first operand `A` is falsy (e.g., `0`), React Compiler renders the falsy value as a text node instead of rendering nothing. ## Reproduction **Repro repo:** https://github.com/famameilin/repro-react-compiler-0-bug **Environment:** - React 19.2.4 - react-dom 19.2.4 - babel-plugin-react-compiler 1.0.0 - @vitejs/plugin-react 6.0.1 - Vite 8.0.1 **Repro code:** ```tsx function HeroPanel({ totalPages }: { totalPages?: number }) { const onPageChange = (page: number) => { console.log('page change to', page); }; return (
{totalPages && totalPages > 1 && onPageChange && (
分页内容
)}
); } // Usage: ``` **Expected:** When `totalPages = 0`, nothing is rendered after the button (because `0 && ...` short-circuits to `0`, and React should not render falsy values as text). **Actual:** The number `0` is rendered as a text node after the button. ## Step-by-Step Analysis 1. `totalPages = 0` (falsy) 2. Expression: `{totalPages && totalPages > 1 && onPageChange && (
...
)}` 3. JavaScript evaluates: `0 && false && undefined && ...` → short-circuits to `0` 4. React receives `0` as the expression result 5. Instead of treating `0` as "nothing to render", React renders it as a text node ## Workaround Replace `&&` with ternary operator: ```tsx {totalPages && totalPages > 1 && onPageChange ? (
分页内容
) : null} ``` ## Related Issues This may be related to [#33181](https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/33181) — `status && ` causes hooks mismatch, which also involves conditional rendering with `&&` and the React Compiler. ## Tags - `Component: React Compiler` - `Type: Bug`

Hello!

I'm a frontend engineer at Grafana, currently investigating excessive/unexpected memory usage.

Grafana is very data-heavy, users run arbitrary queries against databases, and it all ends up in the browser. The existing architecture and plugin/extension ecosystem of Grafana relies on passing this data through a prop to the panel components. We cannot break this contract, so pulling the data out of React props/state is not possible without breaking an enormous amount of existing code that relies on this contract / API.

This was raised back in 2018 in https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/14380, with tl;dr that this was a known design tradeoff of Fiber. however, the issue was stale-closed with no definitive statement from the core team whether this behavior is something that cannot be mitigated.

I don't know the details of the implementation, but it seems odd that once rendering has settled that the old fiber state cannot be released so it can be effectively GC'd.

title: [Feature Request]: Add fetch and Server-Sent Events supports
Performance: RSC rendering pipeline performance analysis
body:
React version: `19.3.0-canary-c0d218f0-20260324` and uhh, [a custom fork](https://github.com/switz/react/pull/2)

## Steps To Reproduce

1. first set of benchmarks are in this repo: https://github.com/switz/rsc-benchmarks
2. second set are based on my fork implementing a fused rsc pipeline renderer (one pass, fizz takes on more responsibility - [preview here](https://github.com/switz/react/pull/2))

<!-- Link to code example: -->

## Some Background

I am working on a new RSC-based framework. There's been a lot of recent discussion around react-based frameworks' performance in what are generally not representative of real world performance (aren't all web benchmarks?), but they did uncover some serious gaps. RSC performance is honestly _sufficient_ for most use-cases, but it could be much more efficient and gets very throttled very quickly.

I spent a lot of time digging into RSC rendering throughput today+yesterday with claude. Both in next and outside of next (w/ my new framework, some pure react, etc.). I found two small perf wins in both Fizz and Flight ([sent a PR for Fizz](https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/36139)), but they are minimal in comparison to the two below. I spent most of the day debugging real world scenarios: code running on the same k8s cluster across the same apps in different contexts (next, my framework, etc.) all running through real-world networks. I then dropped down to baseline benchmarks to try and isolate the problems which reflected my real-world testing.

This is all based on single core, single threaded rendering. If I got anything wrong here, if I shoved my foot in my mouth, if I over-dramatized the situation, please tell me. I'm not an expert in web throughput engineering, cpu architectures, or javascript/react internals. I'm just a long-time software engineer who's having way too much fun building my own framework on what I consider to be the most complete web architecture.

Bug: Malformed `private` field in react-devtools-fusebox package.json
body:
**Bug: Malformed `private` field in react-devtools-fusebox package.json**

Current Behavior

The `package.json` file for `react-devtools-fusebox` uses a **string** for the `private` field instead of a **boolean**:

**Location** [`[packages/react-devtools-fusebox/package.json](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-devtools-fusebox/package.json)`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-devtools-fusebox/package.json)

```json
{
  "private": "true",  //  Should be: "private": true
}
```

### Expected Behavior

According to the [[npm package.json specification](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package.json#private)](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package.json#private), the `private` field must be a **boolean**, not a string:

```json
{
  "private": true,  // Correct
}
```

### Impact

This causes failures in package scanning tools that validate package metadata:

-  **ScanCode.io** pipeline fails when scanning `pkg:github/facebook/react@v19.2.1`
- Type validation error: `'"true" value must be either True or False.'`
- Non-compliant with npm specification

**Related upstream issues:**
- [[aboutcode-org/scancode.io#1986](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode.io/issues/1986)](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode.io/issues/1986) - Pipeline failure report
- [[aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit#4631](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit/issues/4631)](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit/issues/4631) - Root cause analysis
- [[aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit#4635](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit/pull/4635)](https://github.com/aboutcode-org/scancode-toolkit/pull/4635) - Defensive fix to handle malformed data

While downstream tools are adding workarounds, the source data should comply with the npm specification.

### Reproduction

## Description
The `ReactProfilerTimer.js` module currently uses a set of global variables (`transitionStartTime`, `transitionUpdateTime`, `transitionUpdateType`, etc.) to track performance metrics for transitions.

This implementation assumes only one transition is being tracked at a time. However, with concurrent rendering, multiple transitions can be in progress simultaneously in different lanes.

There is an explicit TODO in the code acknowledging this issue:

```javascript
// packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactProfilerTimer.js

// TODO: This should really be one per Transition lane.
export let transitionClampTime: number = -0;
export let transitionStartTime: number = -1.1; // First startTransition call before setState.
export let transitionUpdateTime: number = -1.1; // First transition setState scheduled.
```
## Impact
When multiple concurrent transitions occur, the following issues arise:

1. **Data Overwrites:** Concurrent transitions will overwrite each other's timing data in these global variables.
2. **Inaccurate Profiling:** `ReactFiberWorkLoop` will read incorrect start/update times, leading to inaccurate performance profiling data.
3. **Race Conditions:** It may cause race conditions where the wrong transition's data is logged or used for heuristics.

## Proposed Solution
Refactor `ReactProfilerTimer.js` to avoid global state for transition timings.

* **Structure:** Store transition timing data in a structure keyed by the transition lane, such as `Map<Lane, TransitionTimers>`.
* **Implementation:** The `ReactFiberWorkLoop` and other consumers should be updated to pass the relevant `Lane` when recording or reading transition timings, ensuring that data is isolated per transition.

## Affected Files
* `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactProfilerTimer.js`
* `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`

title: Bug: Initialize transition start time in startTransition and startGestureTransition
body:
## Description
Currently, calls to `startTransition` and `startGestureTransition` in `packages/react/src/ReactStartTransition.js` initialize `currentTransition.startTime` to `-1`. There is a TODO comment indicating that this should read the timestamp.

The timestamp is currently lazily set in `ReactFiberWorkLoop.js` when an update is scheduled. This behavior differs from `useTransition`, which correctly sets the start time immediately.

This issue proposes to:

1. Initialize `startTime` using `performance.now()` (falling back to `Date.now()`) directly in `startTransition` and `startGestureTransition`.
2. Remove the lazy initialization logic in `ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`.

This ensures the timestamp accurately reflects when the transition was started, even if updates are processed later.

## Relevant Files
* `packages/react/src/ReactStartTransition.js`
* `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`

## Steps to Reproduce (or verify)
1. Enable `enableTransitionTracing`.
2. Inspect `currentTransition.startTime` immediately after creating a transition via `startTransition`. Ideally, it should hold a valid timestamp instead of `-1`.

title: Bug: Anchor tags do not support autoFocus
body:
Hi team!

React currently doesn't support the `autoFocus` prop for anchor tags. This issue has been raised before, however it was automatically marked as `Stale` and closed: https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/26603

My opinion matches that of the above ticket author: `autofocus` is a [global attribute](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Global_attributes/autofocus) and should work for anchor tags just like it does for buttons, text inputs, etc. It sounds like this was discussed several years ago (https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/11851#issuecomment-351672131), however browser support for the `autoFocus` attribute has greatly matured since 2017. I'm not sure modern browsers even need the current polyfill behaviour?

React version: 18.2.0 (Same behaviour in `main`)

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Add an `a` tag with a `href` value and `autoFocus`.
2. Observe as the anchor tag is not autofocused on page load.

Link to code example: https://codesandbox.io/p/sandbox/strange-ritchie-wc94dy

title: Bug: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity in react
body:
### Summary
A Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) vulnerability was identified in Facebook React within the react-devtools-shared package. The issue exists in the backend/utils.js component, specifically within the regular expressions used for parsing at lines 368, 369, 381, and 417. By providing a specially crafted input string to the DevTools backend, an attacker or a malicious website being inspected can trigger catastrophic backtracking. This leads to excessive CPU consumption and causes the browser tab or the DevTools process to become unresponsive, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).

### Details
https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/68dbd84b61cc2504c30e19f748f59a52d331f851/packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/utils.js#L368
https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/68dbd84b61cc2504c30e19f748f59a52d331f851/packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/utils.js#L369
https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/68dbd84b61cc2504c30e19f748f59a52d331f851/packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/utils.js#L381
https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/68dbd84b61cc2504c30e19f748f59a52d331f851/packages/react-devtools-shared/src/backend/utils.js#L417


### PoC
PoC for `line 368`:
```js
/**
 * ReDoS PoC for regexId: 6 (Validated and Optimized)
 *
 * Target Regex: /\)+$/
 * Dataflow Path: componentStack -> split('\n') -> trim() -> replace(/^\(+/) -> SINK: replace(/\)+$/)
 * Path Constraints: Must pass Chrome stack format check
 * Data Transformations: split('\n'), trim(), replace(/^\(+/, "")
 *
 * Generated Time: 2025-12-02
 * Phase: Phase 3 - Optimized (2 iterations)
 * Status: VALIDATED SUCCESS
 *
 * === VALIDATION RESULTS ===
 * Phase 2 Result: FAILED (Not reaching target Sink)
 * Phase 3 Iterations: 2
 *
 * Iteration 1: Added ':' to suffix to satisfy path constraint (url.indexOf(':') !== -1)
 *   Result: Reached Sink but insufficient time (1.455s < 2000ms)
 *
 * Iteration 2: Increased repeatTimes from 80,000 to 200,000
 *   Result: SUCCESS - Sink execution time

title: Bug: ViewTransition can't be isolated
body:
React version:
    "react": "19.2.3",
    "react-dom": "19.2.3",

## Steps To Reproduce

I have a Dialog wrapped with ViewTransition. Inside the dialog I’m using the Streamdown library.

Streamdown updates its blocks using startTransition. As a result, view transitions keep triggering while Streamdown is streaming.

It seems like there’s no way to isolate part of the tree so that startTransition inside the dialog doesn’t trigger transitions outside of it.

I can’t disable ViewTransition on the dialog during streaming, because the dialog needs the close animation.

I think view transitions must be executed somehow explicitly and not via startTransition itself.
Or I need a way like 
```
<Isolate>
  ...startTransitions here would not cause view transitions to start

title: Leave me alone
react-reconciler: flushSync was renamed to flushSyncFromReconciler without deprecation notice
body:
In react-reconciler, the `flushSync` export was renamed to `flushSyncFromReconciler` in PR #28500 (merged April 8, 2024). This is an undocumented breaking change for custom renderers.

**Commit:** https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/28500

According to that PR, custom renderers should now use:
- `reconciler.updateContainerSync()` - to update synchronously
- `reconciler.flushSyncWork()` - to flush pending sync work

However, this migration path is not documented anywhere for custom renderer authors. The change silently causes `flushSync` to be `undefined` with no warning.

**0.29.x API:**
```js
const reconciler = ReactReconciler(hostConfig)
const { flushSync } = reconciler  // works

// Usage
flushSync(() => {
  reconciler.updateContainer(element, container, null, callback)
})
```

**0.31.0+ API:**
```js
const reconciler = ReactReconciler(hostConfig)
const { flushSync } = reconciler  // undefined!

// New intended usage (undocumented):
reconciler.updateContainerSync(element, container, null, callback)
reconciler.flushSyncWork()
```

Could we please:
1. Document the new API for custom renderers in the react-reconciler README
2. Or add a deprecation warning when accessing the old `flushSync` property

This affects custom renderers like @opentui/react that were following the previous patterns.
