title: Docs: CSP guide — a proxy's own response Content-Security-Policy silently replaces the request's, so no nonce is applied
body:
### What is the documentation issue?

The [Content Security Policy guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy) shows a proxy that puts the nonce policy on the request (`NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } })`) and sets the same value on the response. It does not mention that the two must be identical, or at least that the response must not carry a *different* `Content-Security-Policy`.

Headers that a proxy sets on its response are copied onto the request the page is rendered from. In `server/lib/router-utils/resolve-routes.js`, every remaining middleware response header is written to both `resHeaders[key]` and `req.headers[key]`. That happens after the `x-middleware-request-*` overrides are applied. `parseRequestHeaders` in `app-render.js` then reads `headers['content-security-policy'] || headers['content-security-policy-report-only']`.

So a proxy that does something reasonable breaks the nonce:

```ts
// request: the nonce policy, as in the guide
headers.set('content-security-policy', `script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'; ...`)
const response = NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } })
// response: a per-path framing rule, enforced, while the script policy is rolled out as report-only
response.headers.set('Content-Security-Policy', "frame-ancestors 'none'")
response.headers.set('Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only', `script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' ...`)
```

- The response's `frame-ancestors 'none'` replaces the request header.
- `getScriptNonceFromHeader` finds no `script-src` and no `default-src` in it.
- No script gets a nonce.
- Nothing warns. The page renders, and the report-only header reports every Next.js script.

The same happens whenever the enforced response policy lacks the nonce, including the common migration step of an enforced baseline plus a report-only nonce policy. Because `content-security-policy` is read before `content-security-policy-report-only`, the report-only policy is never consulted wh

title: Tag invalidation stops working after the machine sleeps: tagsManifest mixes Date.now() and performance.now()
body:
### Summary

After the host machine sleeps with a Next.js server running, `updateTag` / `revalidateTag` stop invalidating `"use cache"` entries. Every later request is served the entry from before the write, until the server restarts.

Cache entry timestamps and the expiry check read `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`. One of the two tag writers reads `Date.now()` instead, and both write to the same shared `tagsManifest`. On macOS the monotonic clock behind `performance.now()` stops while the machine sleeps, so after a sleep `Date.now()` runs ahead of `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()` by the total sleep time. On our dev server it was 9.6 hours ahead after 12 hours of uptime.

### Where

- `server/lib/cache-handlers/default.js` `updateTags` writes `expired: Math.round(performance.timeOrigin + performance.now())`.
- `server/lib/incremental-cache/file-system-cache.js` `revalidateTag` writes `expired: Date.now()` to the same `tagsManifest`. `revalidateTags` (`server/revalidation-utils.js`) calls it after the handlers, so its value is the one that remains.
- `server/lib/incremental-cache/tags-manifest.external.js` `areTagsExpired` requires `expiredAt <= performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`. With a wall-clock `expiredAt` that is now in the future, the check never passes, and the entry is served indefinitely.

In dev, a custom `cacheHandlers.default` does not avoid it: `setCacheHandler` puts a built-in default handler in front as the tiered front cache, and that front reads the same shared manifest.

This was observed on 16.3.5, and 16.3.6 has the same code.

### Reproduction

1. Any app with `cacheComponents: true`, a `"use cache"` function with `cacheTag("x")`, and a Server Action that writes and calls `updateTag("x")`.
2. Simulate a slept machine with a preload, e.g. `BUN_OPTIONS="--preload=./skew.ts" bun --bun next dev`, where `skew.ts` is:
   ```ts
   const now = performance.now.bind(performance);
   performance.now = () => now() - 10 * 60

body:
## Run info

- Next.js 16.3.6, Turbopack dev (`next dev`), Node 26.10.0, pnpm 12.6.0, Ubuntu 24.04 docker container (self-hosted runner)
- monorepo: app at frontend/apps/web with root catch-all `app/[locale]/[[...slug]]/page.tsx` mapping a 63-page component registry (all marketing/console/portal pages render through this single route)

## Repro

1. `next build` succeeds (full graph compiles in ~3 min, production `next start` serves all catch-all routes in ~0.2-0.3s each)
2. `next dev`, request any catch-all slug (e.g. `/en/used-cars`) → `○ Compiling /[locale]/[[...slug]] ...` appears, then **spins at 200-700% CPU indefinitely (observed 37-44 min, no completion)**
3. Deterministic: reproduced locally and in CI (4 consecutive shard runs); unit tests (2373) and typecheck all pass on the same tree

## Not the cause (bisected/verified)

- pnpm 12.5.1 vs 12.6.0: hangs under both
- next-intl 4.14.6 vs 4.14.7: hangs under both
- Resource limits: containers have NO memory/CPU cgroup limits; host = 64 cores / 251GB RAM with ~200GB free
- The route compiled fine in `next build` (production mode) on the same tree

## Workaround in CI

Mock E2E job marked `continue-on-error: true` (non-mandatory gate); upstream investigation needed.

## Question

Is Turbopack dev-mode compilation of a large catch-all registry route a known limitation? Any config (e.g. `turbopack.root`, memory flags, experimental flags) to avoid the spin?

body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/vercel/next.js

### To Reproduce

I use Next.js to proxy requests to another application through external rewrites. The deployment topology is:

Client HTTPS :443 -> TLS-terminating ingress -> Next.js HTTP :8888 -> backend application

The ingress supplies `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` but does not supply `X-Forwarded-Port`.

The backend receives `X-Forwarded-Port: 8888`, which describes Next.js’s internal listening port rather than the public port used by the client. This causes a backend that trusts forwarded headers to reconstruct the public URL with the wrong port.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

When proxying to another application, Next.js should not assume its internal listening port is the original public port.

In this deployment the public port is 443. If Next.js cannot reliably determine the external port,it should either rely on `X-Forwarded-Proto`, or leave the header absent like its upstream did.

title: instrumentation.ts at the project root runs with next start but is dropped from standalone output when the app is in src/app
body:
### Summary

In a project with `src/app`, an `instrumentation.ts` at the **project root** (not in `src/`):
- is compiled to `.next/server/instrumentation.js` (Turbopack), and
- runs with `next start` (`register()` is called),
- but is **not copied** into `.next/standalone/…/.next/server/`. So standalone deployments never call `register()` or `onRequestError`, and no warning is given.

From reading the build code, `next build` looks for the hook in the parent of the app directory (`src/`), so `hasInstrumentationHook` is false and `copyTracedFiles` skips `instrumentation.js.nft.json`, while Turbopack resolves the root-level file anyway.

Impact for us: production (Firebase App Hosting, standalone output) ran for months without server-side Sentry (`Sentry.init` and `onRequestError` live in `register()`), while it worked in local development and our e2e runs, which use `next start`.

### What we observed (monorepo, Next 16.3.6)

1. The app is in `packages/web/src/app`, and `instrumentation.ts` is in `packages/web/`.
2. `NEXT_PRIVATE_STANDALONE=true next build`: `.next/server/instrumentation.js` exists, but `.next/standalone/packages/web/.next/server/` has no `instrumentation.js`.
3. `next start` logs from `register()`; `node .next/standalone/packages/web/server.js` doesn't.
4. After moving the file to `src/instrumentation.ts`, it's in the standalone output and `register()` runs.

### Expected

The build should behave the same either way: include the hook in standalone output whenever it was compiled, or reject or warn about the root-level file when `src/` is used. Right now it silently works in one mode and not the other.

Environment: Next.js 16.3.6 (Turbopack build), Node 22.

title: Incremental cache writes request-time prerenders to disk with no bound or eviction (OOM on in-memory filesystems)
body:
### Summary

With the default cache handler, every page prerendered at request time (ISR, and Cache Components shells for params or locales outside `generateStaticParams`) is persisted to `.next/server/app` when `isrFlushToDisk` is on, which is the default. The in-memory side is bounded by `cacheMaxMemorySize`, but the disk side has no size limit and nothing ever deletes old entries. On platforms whose filesystem is RAM (Cloud Run, including Firebase App Hosting; other container platforms with tmpfs), that unbounded growth ends in a container OOM kill under crawler traffic.

### Repro sketch

1. An App Router app with `cacheComponents: true`, an `[locale]` segment with many locales, and `generateStaticParams` returning only a few of them.
2. `next build && next start`.
3. Request many distinct locale/param combinations (a crawler does this).
4. `.next/server/app` grows by roughly 0.3–0.6 MB per page (HTML, `.meta`, `.segment.rsc` files) and never shrinks. We saw 864 files / 70 MB in 90 s with a tiny dataset; in production ~1.45 GB filled up in about 2 hours.

With `experimental.isrFlushToDisk: false`, nothing is written and pages are still served from the in-memory LRU.

### Suggestions

- Bound the disk cache (a size or entry limit with LRU eviction), or
- Document `isrFlushToDisk` as essential on in-memory filesystems (it's currently an undocumented experimental flag), ideally in the self-hosting / deploying docs.

Environment: Next.js 16.3.6, Node 22, standalone output.

title: `@next/routing`: a rewrite destination's repeated query key is collapsed to its last value (`searchParams.set` should be `append`)
body:
### Summary

`@next/routing` collapses a rewrite destination's repeated query key to its last value, because it merges destination query params with `URLSearchParams#set` instead of `append`. A page reading `props.query.items` gets the string `"2"` where `next start` gives `["1", "2"]`.

This makes `test/e2e/rewrites-destination-query-array` fail for an adapter deployment while passing under `next start`.

Verified on `16.3.5` and still present on `16.4.0-canary.43`.

### Reproduction

The existing fixture is enough — `test/e2e/rewrites-destination-query-array`:

```js
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  rewrites() {
    return [{ source: '/some-page', destination: '/?items=1&items=2' }]
  },
}
```

The test asserts the index page renders `props.query.items.join(',')` as `1,2`.

- `next start`: `200`, renders `1,2`
- adapter deployment (`NEXT_ENABLE_ADAPTER=1`): `500`, with

```
TypeError: a.query.items.join is not a function
```

because `items` arrived as the string `"2"`.

### Cause

Two call sites in `packages/next-routing`, both iterating a destination's search params and writing each into a target `URL`:

```ts
// packages/next-routing/src/destination.ts:63  (applyDestination)
newUrl.searchParams.set(key, value)

// packages/next-routing/src/resolve-routes.ts:312  (mergeDestinationQueryIntoUrl)
mergedUrl.searchParams.set(key, value)
```

`URLSearchParams#entries()` yields one entry per value, so `?items=1&items=2` iterates twice — and `set` overwrites every existing entry for the key. `items=1` is written, then replaced by `items=2`. `append` is the correct operation here.

The loss happens before anything else can compensate: `toResolvedQuery` (`resolve-routes.ts:288`) builds arrays correctly —

```ts
query[key] = Array.isArray(existing) ? [...existing, value] : [existing, value]
```

— but by the time it runs, the URL only has one `items` entry left.

`next start` is unaffected because it resolves routes with its own in-tree `router-server` rather than `@

title: Adapter `nxtP` route params are decoded twice then split on `/`, corrupting a catch-all segment containing `%2F`
body:
### Summary

Route params handed to an adapter deployment through the `nxtP` query contract are decoded **twice** and then split on `/`. A catch-all segment containing an encoded `/` therefore cannot be recovered, and in the `_next/data` case the corrupted params make `normalizePagePath` throw, producing a 500 where both `next start` and a Vercel deployment render a 200.

`test/e2e/incremental-cache-path-traversal` has an `isAdapterTest` branch that asserts the corrupted shape *together with* `status: 200`. Those two assertions are mutually exclusive, so that branch cannot pass for any adapter.

Verified on `16.3.5` and `16.4.0-canary.43`.

### The double decode, and why nothing on the adapter side can fix it

For `GET /pages-cache/..%2F..%2Fserver-reference-manifest`, an adapter follows the documented contract and passes the capture as a `nxtP` query value. On the way in, `RouteModule.prepare` does two things to it.

`normalizeQueryParams` (`packages/next/src/server/server-utils.ts`) strips the prefix and runs `decodeQueryPathParameter` — a second `decodeURIComponent`, on top of the one the query parser already did:

```ts
query[normalizedKey] = Array.isArray(value)
  ? value.map((v) => decodeQueryPathParameter(v))
  : decodeQueryPathParameter(value)
```

`normalizeDynamicRouteParams` then splits a string repeat param:

```ts
// query values from the proxy aren't already split into arrays
// so make sure to normalize catch-all values
if (value && typeof value === 'string' && defaultRouteRegex!.groups[key].repeat) {
  value = value.split('/')
}
```

Two decodes and a split. There is no string an adapter can put in `nxtPrest` that survives both and yields `['a/b']` for a request to `/pages-cache/a%2Fb`:

- if the value after two decodes contains a `/`, the split fires and you get `['a', 'b']`;
- if it does not contain a `/`, then no element can contain one either, and you get `['a%2Fb']`.

So the contract cannot represent an encoded path delimiter inside a catch-all

title: Turbopack scope hoisting: a circular import inside a merged factory captures a partial namespace, so a client transition crashes while a hard load of the same URL works
body:
### Versions

- next 16.3.5 (Turbopack, `next build`), react 19.3.0
- react-aria-components 1.21.1, react-stately 3.50.0, via @heroui/react 3.2.6
- Windows 11, Node 22

### What happens

In a production build, clicking an in-page link from `/` to `/listings` drops
the page into the error boundary:

```text
TypeError: (0 , h.useOverlayTriggerState) is not a function
```

A hard load of `/listings` renders correctly. `next dev` never shows it.
`next build --webpack` never shows it.

### Mechanism, traced by hooking the Turbopack module runtime

`experimental.turbopackScopeHoisting` is on for `next build` and off in dev. It
merges modules into one factory. Inside a merged factory, an import of a module
that is still initialising returns a snapshot of the exports that module had at
that moment. The importing factory keeps that snapshot in a top-level binding
for the life of the page.

react-aria-components has an import cycle:

```text
TextField          -> useOverlayTriggerState
useOverlayTriggerState -> Dialog (OverlayTriggerStateContext)
Dialog             -> useMenuItem
useMenuItem        -> useOverlayTriggerState   <- snapshot; only `default` present
```

`/` enters the cycle from the `useOverlayTriggerState` side, through a
`TextField`. A hard load of `/listings` enters from the `useMenuItem` side,
through `Select`/`Drawer`, and every binding resolves. The page that paints first
determines which module receives the empty namespace. Webpack is unaffected
because its namespace objects are live getters, not snapshots.

The failing edge is the same in every tree we built; only the entry module
changes. Swapping components does not avoid it, because the order of entry is
what matters.

### Workaround

```ts
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  experimental: {turbopackScopeHoisting: false}
};
```

Measured cost in this app: +51,144 bytes across 26 client chunks (+2.6%
uncompressed), build 974 ms to 1,283 ms.

### Exp

title: [dev] Uncaught `TypeError: Failed to execute 'measure' on 'Performance': '<Component>' cannot have a negative time stamp`
body:
### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Next.js | 16.3.3 (webpack) — **also present in 16.3.5**, verified by inspecting the published bundle |
| React | 19.2.8 (bundled `react-server-dom-webpack`) |
| Browser | Chrome (any Chromium) |
| Mode | `next dev`, App Router |

### Summary

In development, when an RSC render ends with the **root chunk rejected**, the flight client flushes
component timings and calls `performance.measure` with an `end` that is **not clamped**, while `start`
**is** clamped. Because the debug-channel timings and `response._timeOrigin` are read from two different
clock frames, `end` can be a large negative number, and Chromium throws:

```
Uncaught TypeError: Failed to execute 'measure' on 'Performance': 'ChatIndexPage' cannot have a negative time stamp.
```

The throw is uncaught and crashes the dev overlay.

### Where

`node_modules/next/dist/compiled/react-server-dom-webpack/cjs/react-server-dom-webpack-client.browser.development.js`

| line | branch | `end` guarded? |
|---|---|---|
| 1332, 1385, 1432, 4037, 4197 | normal paths | ✅ `0 < endTime` / `0 <= endTime` |
| **3907** (`end` at **3909**) | **errored** | ❌ none |
| **4165** (`end` at **4167**) | **aborted** | ❌ none |

```js
performance.measure(measureName, {
  start: 0 > startTime ? 0 : startTime,   // ← clamped
  end: childrenEndTime,                   // ← passed through unclamped
  detail: { devtools: { color: "error", tooltipText: entryName + " Errored", ... } }
});
```

Call site in our repro:

```
at Performance.measure
at flushComponentPerformance (...client.browser.development.js:3907:35)
at flushComponentPerformance (...3822:27)
at flushInitialRenderPerformance (...4268:11)
```

Captured by wrapping `Performance.prototype.measure` on a real app:

| quantity | observed value |
|---|---|

| `response._timeOrigin` | **−16490.951 ms** |

body:
### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

https://github.com/Aabshir/next-refresh-query-repro

(Re-file of #99026, which was auto-closed for missing a reproduction link. The repro is now a public repository; it contains only the minimal app, no other code.)

### To Reproduce

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Aabshir/next-refresh-query-repro
cd next-refresh-query-repro
npm install
npm run build
npm start   # production build required; next dev does not exercise the cached path
```

The page renders a `#stamp` timestamp (`export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"`) and a button that POSTs a mutation and then calls `router.refresh()`. The page deliberately streams (a ~12 KB filler block + a Suspense chunk that resolves after 300 ms) so the Flight response arrives in multiple chunks.

1. Open `/` (no query string), click **Mutate + refresh** several times.
2. Open `/?status=draft` (any query string; the page never reads `searchParams`), click **Mutate + refresh** several times.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

Expected: the stamp updates on every click in both cases — `router.refresh()` should always discard the client cache and re-render the current URL from the server.

Actual (see version matrix below): on most Next 16 versions the stamp **never updates**. CDP network capture shows that after the mutation POST, **no `_rsc` fetch is initiated at all** for the refresh — the router silently keeps/reapplies its stale cached payload. In a real application the symptom is: the mutation persists server-side, the UI shows pre-mutation data indefinitely, and only a hard reload fixes it.

### Version matrix (same repro, production build, automated browser, 3–6 rounds per cell)

| Version | `/` (no query) | `/?status=draft` |
|---|---|---|
| 16.1.7 | ❌ stale | ❌ stale |
| **16.2.12** | ✅ fresh every time | ❌ stale every time |
| 16.3.5 (latest stable at time of writing) | ❌ stale | ❌ stale |
| 16.4.0-canary.37 (latest canary at time of writing) | ❌ stale | ❌ stale |

title: Turbopack dev server reports Ready with a partial route graph; missing routes never register (persists for the life of the process)
body:
### Summary

On a CI runner, a freshly started Next.js 16.3.5 dev server (Turbopack) can report `Ready in ~300ms` while having registered only a **subset** of the application's routes. Requests to the missing subtrees return the framework's HTML 404 page immediately (tens of ms — not a compile window), and the missing entries **never register later**: the state persists for the life of the process. Restarting the server is the only recovery.

### Why this is worth fixing at source

A CI gate that runs `next dev` and starts testing when the port answers is running its assertions against a possibly-incomplete route graph. In our case the missing tier produced 404s that looked, in the test assertions, like fixture-absence failures — sending the first investigation toward the test fixtures rather than the server.

### Environment

- Next.js **16.3.5** (Turbopack dev)
- Node **22**
- GitHub Actions `ubuntu-latest`, runner image `20260831.293.1`
- App Router project, ~40 routes including dynamic segments and nested API routes (shape: `/api/reports/daily/[date]/{csv,pdf,status,manifest}/route.ts`)

### Evidence — two captures, same runner type, hours apart

**Capture A — original failure.** The `[date]` subdirectory routes (`csv`, `pdf`, `status`, `manifest`) returned framework 404s for the whole run. The parent `[date]` route and the top-level `/api/reports/dates` worked; a nested dynamic *page* route worked. Failing assertions exhausted retries within ~1.4s at ~60–100ms per attempt — an instant refusal, not a compile stall. Fresh runner, fresh `.next`, so not a warm-cache artifact.

**Capture B — instrumented reproduction** (three fresh dev servers in sequence on one runner). Servers 1 and 2 served every route. Server 3 answered `Ready in 311ms`, then framework-404'd the entire `/api/reports/*` API tier **and** the `/reporting/daily` page, while `/login` worked in the same process. Present from the first request, never healed: ~400 re-fetches over ~7 minutes, framework 4

### Link to the code that reproduces this issue

Minimal reproduction, App Router, four lines:

```tsx
// app/gone/page.tsx
import { notFound } from "next/navigation";

export default function Page() {
  notFound();
}
```

With `app/not-found.tsx` present, run `next build && next start`, then:

```bash
curl -s http://localhost:3000/gone | grep -c '<main'   # 0
curl -s http://localhost:3000/no-such-route | grep -c '<main'   # 1
```

### To Reproduce

1. Add the page above and any `not-found.tsx`.
2. `next build && next start` (production — this does not reproduce in dev).
3. `curl` the route that calls `notFound()`. The response is **404 with an empty `<body>`**.
4. `curl` a route that simply does not exist. The response is 404 **with the `not-found.tsx` markup**.

### Current vs. Expected behavior

**Expected:** a `notFound()` 404 serves the same `not-found.tsx` markup that an unmatched URL serves.

**Current:** a `notFound()` 404 serves `<html id="__next_error__"><head></head><body></body></html>`. The content exists only in the RSC flight payload, so it appears after hydration. With JavaScript unavailable the page is permanently blank.

An unmatched URL is unaffected, and that asymmetry appears to be the mechanism: an unmatched URL is resolved to `/_not-found` and rendered as a *page*, whereas `notFound()` is a thrown error.

`HTTPAccessFallbackBoundary` is a client component, and React does not run error boundaries during server rendering, so the throw escapes the whole Fizz render. `app-render.js` then catches it and serves a hardcoded document whose body is `null` outside development:

```js

jsx("html", {
  id: "__next_error__",
  children: [
    jsx("head", {}),
    jsx("body", {
      children: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' && err
        ? jsx("template", { "data-next-error-message": err.message, /* … */ })
        : null,
    }),
  ],
})
```

title: next dev rewrites tsconfig.json with a doubled '.next/dev/dev/types' include when NODE_ENV=test
body:
### Summary

`next dev` rewrites `tsconfig.json` on every start when `NODE_ENV` is set to `test`, appending an include glob with a doubled path segment:

```
- include was updated to add '.next/dev/dev/types/**/*.ts'
```

`.next/dev/dev` is never created, so the glob matches nothing — but the file is modified on every run. Revert it and the next `next dev` puts it back.

Nothing warns, because `test` is on the standard-env list (`bin/next.ts:96`) and `bin/next.ts:119` preserves an already-set `NODE_ENV`. An ambient `NODE_ENV=test` is common: Vitest and Jest set it, and CI often exports it for the whole job.

### The mismatch

Two places decide "am I in dev mode", from two different signals.

**`distDir` is derived from the build phase** — `packages/next/src/server/config.ts:1757`:

```ts
if (phase === PHASE_DEVELOPMENT_SERVER) {
  result.distDir = join(result.distDir, 'dev')
}
```

**Whether to strip or append that `/dev` is derived from `NODE_ENV`** — `packages/next/src/lib/typescript/type-paths.ts:19`:

```ts
typeGlobPatterns.push(
  process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'
    ? // In dev, distDir is "{distDir}/dev", so also include "{distDir}/types"
      `${distDirPosix.replace(/\/dev$/, '')}/types/**/*.ts`
    : // In build, distDir is "{distDir}", so also include "{distDir}/dev/types"
      `${distDirPosix}/dev/types/**/*.ts`
)
```

The comments state the assumption exactly: each branch believes it knows the shape of `distDir`. But the caller (`writeConfigurationDefaults.ts:291`) passes the phase-derived value. `next dev` with `NODE_ENV=test` is phase-dev (so `distDir` is already `.next/dev`) while taking the non-development branch, which appends `/dev` a second time without checking whether it is already there.

Isolated, with no app involved:

```js
const path = require('path')
const { getTypeDefinitionGlobPatterns: g } = require('next/dist/lib/typescript/type-paths.js')
const distDir = path.join('.next', 'dev')   // exactly what config.ts produces in dev pha

title: Turbopack: nested next/dynamic gets no SSR stylesheet link, causing FOUC and layout shift in App Router
body:
### Summary

In App Router with a Turbopack build, a `next/dynamic` call declared **inside a module that is itself loaded via `next/dynamic`** ends up with no stylesheet link in the server-rendered HTML. Its CSS is fetched by the client chunk loader after hydration instead.

What we can see from the outside:

- the component is server-rendered with markup, but its stylesheet is not in the HTML
- in the built output, that CSS chunk is in neither the route's `entryCSSFiles` nor `react-loadable-manifest.json`
- in the DOM it shows up only after hydration, as a plain `<link>` with no `data-precedence` and `renderBlockingStatus: "non-blocking"`
- a `next/dynamic` at the first level, in the same tree, does get `<link rel="stylesheet" precedence="dynamic">`

Result: the section paints unstyled and snaps into place when the CSS lands — a flash of unstyled content and a large layout shift.

This looks at odds with the intent described in Next's own source, though we may be misreading how these pieces are meant to fit together:

- `packages/next/src/shared/lib/lazy-dynamic/loadable.tsx`: `/* During SSR, we need to preload the CSS from the dynamic component to avoid flash of unstyled content */`
- `packages/next/src/shared/lib/lazy-dynamic/preload-chunks.tsx`: `// For stylesheets we actually need to render the CSS because nothing else is going to do it`

### Where we suspect this comes from (guess, not a diagnosis)

We're application developers and don't know the Turbopack internals, so please treat this as a pointer rather than a root cause. While looking for an explanation, one thing stood out to us: `PreloadChunks` renders a stylesheet link from `opts.modules` looked up in `reactLoadableManifest`, so anything absent from that manifest cannot get a link — and the affected chunks are exactly the ones missing from it.

Searching for why they might be missing, we noticed the DFS in `crates/next-api/src/module_graph.rs` (tag `v16.3.4`, around lines 204-210) records a dynamic ent

Support change requests in `future.services.update_flag`.

title: Stale flags remain stale after being modified
body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Today our _feature flag staleness_ detection is rather simple: once _any_ of a feature's versions is older than a [configurable] period, the feature will automatically earn a "Stale" tag. The mechanism ignores whether the flag is being actively maintained, and the tag is never removed.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

One would expect that a feature flag isn't marked as stale unless it receives no updates within [`Project.stale_flags_limit_days`](https://github.com/Flagsmith/flagsmith/blob/9e0f142fdbbfb8dbd61362c23af0588f4311309f/api/projects/models.py#L109-L112).

A stale flag being updated should also have the tag removed.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- A workaround is to tag the feature "Permanent", but it's not a good solution.
- It's also possible to extend the default period from 30d to a longer time.

### Additional context

- Reported by a customer via the Feature Lifecycle dashboard (#7001).
- Staleness only runs for projects with v2 feature versioning on Scale-Up/Enterprise plans.
- Original design: #184. Related: #6125.

title: Rollout summary legend renders variant keys in body type
body:
Follows #8385, which put variant keys in mono at the four surfaces where they render as JSX. The rollout summary legend still shows them in body type.

`RolloutSummary.tsx:69` renders `arm.label`, which comes from `getRolloutSummaryRows` (`rollout.ts:93`) resolving `option.key || getDefaultVariantKey(index)` into a plain string. `rollout.ts:123` builds a summary string from the same labels.

It was left out of #8385 because it is not a component swap:

- `RolloutSummaryRow` is `{ label: string, percentage: number }`, with no way to say a label is a variant key
- the legend mixes keys with a prose `Control` entry, so it cannot be blanket-monospaced
- the label doubles as the React key and as `barSegments[].key`

So it needs that type to carry the distinction, threaded through `getTrafficSegments`, then `VariantKey` at the render site.

title: Frontend: Redux Toolkit error #38 thrown during RTK Query refetch on the features page
body:
Sentry: [FLAGSMITH-FRONTEND-59J](https://flagsmith.sentry.io/issues/7690231267/)

## What happens

An unhandled promise rejection is thrown from an RTK Query `refetch` on the features page:

fetch  https://api.flagsmith.com/api/v1/environments/UMNS4AmLfMe828RGgTNx4d/edge-identities/1353ae6f-cd02-4...

## Stack

```
/static/main.804dff76976db6b8.js   ?
/static/main.804dff76976db6b8.js   cb
/static/main.804dff76976db6b8.js   refetch

title: Agree the panel surface, then migrate Panel to tokens
body:
A bordered surface with a radius, a background and sometimes a shadow appears all over the app, and no two implementations agree.

| Where | radius | padding | shadow |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `experiments/MetricsTrendChart` | xl | 20px | sm |
| `experiments/MetricsComparisonTable` | xl | 12px | sm |
| `experiments/VariationTable` | xl | 12px | sm |
| `experiments/MetricsTable` | lg | 10px | none |
| `experiments/CreateMetricForm` | md | 14px | none |
| `pages/usage` sections | lg | 24px | none |

Fourteen files hand-roll it in SCSS with `border: 1px solid var(--color-border-default)`, including `base/Chip`, `base/SelectableCard`, `base/grid/ContentCard`, eight under `experiments/`, and the onboarding connect panel.

## There is already a component for this

`base/grid/Panel.tsx` renders a bordered surface with an optional heading row carrying a title and an action, which is the shape most of the hand-rolled ones are reaching for.

It gets avoided because it is pre-token: a class component rendering `.panel`, themed through a `.dark` ancestor selector and `$panel-*` SCSS variables rather than custom properties. `components/Card.tsx` is a thinner version of the same thing and renders `panel panel-default`, a class no stylesheet defines.

The drift above is the symptom. Everyone routed around the legacy component and picked their own values.

**Blast radius:** `Panel` has 16 consumers, `.panel` appears directly in 15 more files, `Card` has 3 consumers across 6 usages.

## What needs deciding first

One radius, one padding, one shadow-or-not for a panel surface. Nothing else can start until that is settled, and it is a design decision rather than an engineering task.

## Then

- express it once, as a token group or a single utility, so a component and a hand-rolled stylesheet can both reach it
- point `Panel` at it and fold `Card` in, since `Card` is a `Panel` without a heading
- let the 14 hand-rolled surfaces adopt incrementally, not in one sweep: the dark-mode m

title: Show which usage notifications we send and to whom
body: **Scoped down.** A static page that states who is notified and at what thresholds. Choosing your own is deferred, along with the API it depends on. **Goal.** Someone can see when we will contact them about usage, and who will hear about it, without asking support. **Scope** - list the thresholds we notify on: 75, 90, 100, 120, 200, 300, 400 and 500 (`api/organisations/constants.py`) - say who receives them. Below 100% only organisation admins are emailed. At 100% and above everyone in the organisation is (`api/organisations/task_helpers.py`) - keep the "what counts as an API call" reference on the page - copy makes clear we never cut off API access at any of these. They are notifications, not limits Both facts are available today, so this needs no backend work and can ship ahead of the rest of the epic. **Done when** - the page lists all eight thresholds, not a subset - the admins-only rule below 100% is stated, since it is a common support question **Deferred, not cancelled** - adding, editing and removing thresholds - channel choices beyond what we already send - the per-organisation notification configuration API this depends on
